context: A building site has opened next to the block of flats where you live. The construction company has written to residents.

paragraphs: Work on the new office block beside your building began this week and will continue for about eight months. Machinery will operate from seven in the morning until seven in the evening, six days a week.
We recognise that this will cause disturbance and we want to limit it as far as we can. Please tell us what problems you are experiencing and what we could do to help.

task11: Write a message to your friend who lives in the same block. Write about your feelings and what you are going to do about the noise.
task12: Write an email to the site manager. Explain the problems the work is causing you and suggest what the company could do to reduce the disturbance.
part2_question: Should cities build upwards or outwards?

task11: How are you coping with the drilling? It starts at seven and I have not slept properly all week. I am writing to the site manager to ask for a later start on Saturdays. Would you sign it with me? A letter from several flats carries more weight.
task12: Thank you for writing to residents about the work beside our building. I appreciate being told in advance, but I must explain the difficulty the current hours are causing.

I work night shifts at the hospital and sleep during the morning. Drilling from seven o'clock makes that impossible, and after a week I am already exhausted. Several neighbours with young children have the same problem. The windows on this side of the building are single-glazed, which makes the noise considerably worse.

Three things would help considerably. Could the noisiest work begin at nine rather than seven, could Saturday work finish at one o'clock, and could you publish a weekly schedule so that residents know when the loudest days are coming?
part2: As cities grow, every planner faces the same choice: add towers in the centre or new districts at the edge. I believe building upwards is, on the whole, the wiser option.

Density is the main argument. A tall building houses hundreds of families on the footprint of a few houses, which keeps journeys short and makes buses, schools and clinics affordable to run. Sprawl does the opposite: it eats farmland, forces everyone into a car and leaves the outer districts dependent on roads that are permanently congested.

I do not pretend the case is one-sided. Towers can be badly built and badly managed, they overshadow streets, and families with small children often want a garden rather than a balcony on the fourteenth floor. Tall buildings are also far cheaper to heat, because each flat shares walls with its neighbours rather than losing heat on every side.

The sensible answer is height with conditions: good design, real parks at ground level, and a limit on how far a city is allowed to spread before it is obliged to build up instead. Where towers have failed, it has almost always been poor maintenance rather than height that was to blame.
